name: Sasaki
description: Sasaki is a North Korean climbing card game for four players. Players try to get rid of all cards; temporary partnerships are determined by the two red 10s. The game is named after the combination 44A (two Fours and one Ace).

overview.description: Sasaki is a North Korean climbing card game for four players. Players try to get rid of all cards; temporary partnerships are determined by the two red 10s. The game is named after the combination 44A (two Fours and one Ace).

history.origins: This climbing game for four players is said to be very popular in North Korea. It is named after the special combination Sasaki (사사끼), meaning 44A (two Fours and one Ace). It is closely related to the Chinese game Red Ten (红十) but it is not clear which game is based on the other.
timeline: Modern Era: Continues to be played worldwide

setup.players: Four players. Temporary partnerships: the two players holding the red 10s (Heart 10 and Diamond 10) are partners; if one player holds both, that player plays alone against the other three.
setup.deck: 48-card deck: standard international deck with all Twos and Jokers removed. Ranks from high to low: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3.
setup.dealing: No dealer. Cards are shuffled and fanned face down; each player in turn takes the top card until all 48 are taken (12 cards each). Play is counter-clockwise.
setup.equipment: Standard 48-card deck (no 2s, no jokers). Score sheet (optional). Table space.

rules.objective: Get rid of all your cards before the others. Help your partner (the other holder of a red 10) when possible. Players are ranked 1st–4th by order of going out; team scores depend on placement.
rules.gameplay: 1. Deal: 12 cards each from a fanned pile (no dealer). 2. Partnerships: Holders of the two red 10s are partners; one holding both plays alone. 3. First lead: Holder of Heart 3 (day) or Spade 3 (evening) may lead any single or valid combination. 4. Play: Counter-clockwise; each player must beat the previous play with a higher same-type combination (or a special combination) or pass. When three pass in a row, the last player to play leads. 5. Special combinations: Triplet, Sasaki (44A), Four of a Kind, Pig (two red 10s; beatable only by Black Pig). 6. Jata/kkota: A single can be beaten by a pair of same rank (jata); that pair can be beaten only by the fourth card of that rank (kkota). 7. End: When three players are out, the last shows any red 10s; scoring by team placement.
keyRules: Ordinary combinations (single, pair, sequence) are beaten by a higher same-type same-length combination or any special combination.
Special combinations beat ordinary ones; Pig (two red 10s) beats everything except Black Pig (two black 10s).
Running: Exposing a red 10 before play doubles the deal score; the other team may call stop to quadruple it.

strategy.basic: Play low cards early when you have the lead; save high combinations to beat opponents. Coordinate with your partner when you know who they are.
strategy.intermediate: Track which special combinations (triplets, Sasaki, four of a kind, Pig) have been played. Use jata (pair on a single) to steal the lead when the next player would otherwise play a strong combo.
strategy.advanced: Decide when to run (expose red 10s) to double stakes; opponents may call stop to quadruple. If alone with both red 10s, time your Pig to go out or force passes.
tips: When you hold a red 10, exposing it reveals partnerships and doubles the score for the deal.
After a kkota (fourth card), that player leads; use that to dump low cards or start a new combination type.

variations.name: Double sequence (ssangka)
variations.description: An extra ordinary combination: three or more consecutive pairs (e.g. 4-4-5-5-6-6). Beaten only by a higher double sequence of the same length or by four of a kind or Pig; not by triplet or Sasaki. Some allow double sequence to jata a single sequence of the same ranks, then a single sequence can kkota the double sequence.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Engine overrides for double-sequence combination type not yet modeled.

variations.name: Red 10s as last two cards
variations.description: Some allow a player whose last two cards are the two red 10s to play them as a Pig to beat any combination and go out. Others play that a lone player with both red 10s as last two cannot play them as a pair at all, only as single cards.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Rule override for endgame Pig use not yet modeled.

scoring.description: Team placement scoring: 1st+2nd place team +2 each; 1st+3rd +1 each; 2nd+4th or 1st+4th no score; 3rd+4th -2 each. Lone player vs three: 1st +6, 4th -3; others 0 or -2/+1. Scores doubled if red 10s exposed (running), quadrupled if other team calls stop. Scores sum to zero; often played for stakes.
scoring.winCondition: First player to empty their hand wins the round; game ends after agreed number of deals or when a player reaches the target score.

synthesis.shortDescription: Sasaki (44A) is a North Korean four-player climbing game. Partners are determined by the two red 10s; players shed cards using singles, pairs, sequences, and special combinations including Sasaki (two 4s and an Ace) and Pig (two red 10s).
